quote: But we do not have such direct control over our beliefs. You cannot make yourself believe the sky is green by an act of will.
content: True, and beside the point, because the position the essay attacks does not require direct control. Doxastic involuntarism is the standard view; what the self-deception literature adds is that indirect control is everywhere. People steer belief by choosing what to attend to, whom to listen to, which evidence to double-check and when to stop, and the result is systematically inflated beliefs about their own abilities, control and prospects that are held sincerely and are demonstrably functional (Taylor & Brown 1988; Kunda 1990). No one thinks "and now I will irrationally believe"; the brain does the choosing below the level at which the essay's argument operates. The essay refutes the version of second-order rationality in which the self-deception is announced, and leaves untouched the version that actually occurs, which is the one the essay's opponents were describing.

quote: Be irrationally optimistic about your driving skills, and you will be happily unconcerned where others sweat and fear. You won’t have to put up with the inconvenience of a seat belt.
content: The illusion of superior driving skill is real, with most drivers rating themselves above the median (Svenson 1981), and the rest of the story is invented. Nothing in that literature connects self-rated skill to seat-belt refusal, and the overconfident majority buckle up at the same rates as everyone else. The chain from optimism to crash is a fable in which the moral has been chosen first. The tradeoff the essay says cannot be made without debiasing is made constantly by ordinary people using actuarial rules, seat belts, speed limits, that do not depend on accurate self-assessment at all; that is the point of a rule. And the optimism bias itself is now contested at the level of measurement, with the belief-updating asymmetry that was its strongest evidence attributed to a statistical artifact (Shah et al. 2016).

quote: Maybe there are stupid happy people out there. Maybe they are happier than you are.
content: The data exist and they do not describe stupid happy people. In a large English population survey, lower measured intelligence was associated with lower, not higher, happiness, an association mostly accounted for by income, health and daily functioning (Ali et al. 2013); at the individual level within normal ranges the correlation between intelligence and life satisfaction is close to zero. The "happiness of stupidity" that the essay treats as a closed door is not a documented phenomenon, and the friend who said it was real was wrong on the evidence. The essay's alternative, that a rationalist's happiness "may prove greater in the end," is offered with no evidence either, and the rationalist community's own later surveys of its members' wellbeing are not the kind of data that could settle it. Both halves of the comparison are folklore.
